extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulemakers; state and tribal certifying authorities; environmental lawyers and advocacy organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Formal public-comment legal analysis evaluating EPA's proposed revisions to Clean Water Act Section 401 regulations and articulating legal, procedural, and environmental standards the rule must meet. Focuses on statutory interpretation, federalism, administrative record, procedural requirements, and environmental/tribal justice obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect state and tribal primary authority under the Clean Water Act
rubrics_metrics.description: States have 'the primary responsibilities and rights … to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution.' 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b). Section 401 provides states and tribes with authority to impose conditions necessary to ensure compliance with water quality requirements, and, where necessary, the authority to block projects outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must not usurp or curtail state and tribal authority; revisions cannot undermine the statute’s federalist allocation of power. Cites S.D. Warren, PUD No. 1, and the view that federal agencies have no authority to second-guess such state decisions (e.g., Sierra Club v. U.S. Army Corps). Any rule that restricts or supplants state/tribal decisionmaking is unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not narrow Section 401(d) to conditions only on point-source 'discharges'; conditions may apply to the 'applicant' generally
rubrics_metrics.description: PUD No. 1 held that limitations imposed under Section 401(d) need not pertain only to the discharge that triggered Section 401; the text refers to the compliance of the applicant, not the discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot lawfully reinterpret 401(d) to eliminate states' ability to impose conditions on broader applicant activities (e.g., instream flow requirements). The Supreme Court's Chevron step 1 reasoning precludes EPA adopting an interpretation that contradicts PUD No. 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'discharge' broadly—Section 401 is not limited to point source discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court in S.D. Warren defined 'discharge' as a 'flowing or issuing out.' The statutory definitions distinguish 'discharge' from 'discharge of a pollutant' (the latter defined to require a point source), demonstrating that 'discharge' is broader than point-source additions of pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA should not limit Section 401's trigger to only point source discharges; doing so would conflict with statutory structure and case law (S.D. Warren; AES Sparrows Point).

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must show a factual, record-based problem and a rational basis for the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must identify and justify the problem it claims to fix; EPA has not shown the alleged problem exists across Section 401 cases and has relied on a handful of high-profile denials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administrative record must contain evidence that current regulations cause undue interference, and that the proposed changes will actually address those problems without degrading water quality. EPA's Economic Analysis that 'denials are uncommon' and that delays are often due to incomplete requests undermines the asserted justification; EPA must provide stronger record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule must protect water quality and cannot be designed to promote fossil fuel infrastructure at water’s expense
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clean Water Act's purpose is to 'restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation's waters.' The Proposed Rule appears motivated to 'encourag[e]' and 'promot[e]' energy infrastructure per Executive Order 13868.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cannot promulgate rules whose purpose is to facilitate infrastructure when that purpose conflicts with the CWA’s protective mandate. Any policy aimed at speeding approvals must demonstrate equal or better protection of water quality than the existing regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess impacts across all types of Section 401 usages, not only fossil-fuel projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 401 applies to thousands of permits annually across many project types; EPA focused narrowly on three pipeline and one coal-export example while ignoring the many non-fossil projects that rely on 401 (e.g., mining, hydroelectric dams).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking analyses must evaluate effects on mining, hydroelectric, and other projects where 401 conditions are critical. EPA must quantify scope (e.g., 4,266 individual and 58,766 general permits per year per its ICR) and evaluate downstream consequences on diverse project categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain states' ability to address non-point-source and indirect impacts (sediment, flows, thermal, groundwater, long-term treatment, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities for which certification is required often have serious water quality impacts unrelated to direct point-source discharges—e.g., increases in sediment loads; reduced stream flows; thermal loading from riparian removal; destabilized banks; altered groundwater regimes; designation of waters as 'waste treatment systems'; acid mine drainage; perpetual water treatment obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States and tribes must be able to impose conditions addressing these impacts; EPA may not prohibit states from considering such impacts in 401 reviews without undermining water quality protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not impose a heightened burden of proof on states/tribes seeking to deny certification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule would impose novel burdens on states/tribes to justify denials. Section 401 gives states authority to assure compliance; EPA offers no statutory basis to make denials more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the existing allocation of burdens: applicants must show that their projects will comply with applicable water quality requirements; states/tribes may deny where compliance is not demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rules must reflect review realities; EPA must not set arbitrarily short statutory or regulatory timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's proposed arbitrarily short timeframes will make it impossible for states and tribes to determine that applicants have met the burden or to develop appropriate conditions, and will stymie authorized agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time limits should account for real-world information needs, pre-filing timelines, and the need for follow-up requests; unreasonable time constraints risk waivers/denials that erode protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize pre-filing but allow agencies to request additional information after application
rubrics_metrics.description: A meaningful pre-filing process should be considered in setting 'reasonable' review time, but it does not eliminate the certifying agency's ability to seek follow-up information requested during application review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal agency determining the 'reasonable' time for review should consider pre-filing results, materials to be submitted, and applicant commitments, but must still permit follow-up requests when information gaps become apparent during review (FERC practice cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorized agencies must retain flexibility to request additional information (scope, number, and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule would limit the timing and scope of additional requests even when necessary to evaluate applications. Such limits are arbitrary given that gaps often only become apparent after review of initial materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit the certifying authority’s ability to issue follow-up information requests; limits would handicap meaningful review and could force inappropriate waivers or denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA cannot grant federal permitting agencies authority to overrule state/tribal 401 decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every circuit to consider the issue has held that federal agencies have no authority to second-guess state decisions; Section 401 'assure[s] that Federal licensing or permitting agencies cannot override State water quality requirements.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule must preserve the non-preemption and finality of state/tribal 401 decisions and cannot create mechanisms for federal override of conditions or denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must analyze combined/regulatory interactions (e.g., WOTUS changes) before revising 401
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's separate efforts to narrow the definition of 'waters of the United States' will interact with Section 401 administration; EPA must assess and make public how combined revisions will affect 401.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking must include cumulative impact assessment across concurrent rulemakings to avoid unintended reductions in protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with Endangered Species Act Section 7 consultation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 requires consultation with USFWS and NMFS where an agency action may affect listed species or critical habitat; EPA failed to consult for the Proposed Rule despite foreseeable effects from limiting 401 protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before finalizing the rule, EPA must consult and ensure the rule will not jeopardize listed species or adversely modify critical habitat; failure to consult violates ESA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform meaningful Environmental Justice (EJ) analysis per EO 12898 and EPA guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 12,898 requires agencies to identify and address disproportionately high and adverse effects on minority and low-income populations; EPA's bare assertion of 'no potential disproportionately high and adverse human health or environmental effects' lacks analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must conduct rigorous EJ assessments in rulemaking (qualitative or quantitative), identify potential disparate impacts, engage affected communities, and address disproportionate effects in final rulemaking as guided by EPA's EJ 2020 Action Agenda and EJ Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct meaningful government-to-government tribal consultation per EO 13175
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13,175 requires agencies to ensure meaningful and timely input by tribal officials on actions with tribal implications; EPA's outreach was inadequate and after decisions were effectively made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must engage in substantive consultation with tribes, consider tribal waters/TAS issues, evaluate impacts on tribal water quality (noting many tribal waters lack enforceable standards), and hold listening sessions accessible to tribes rather than relying solely on docket comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply rule changes retroactively; limit to prospective application
rubrics_metrics.description: Any changes to Section 401 regulations 'must be prospectively applied to new applications only. Any retroactive application would be deeply inappropriate and cause a regulatory nightmare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state in final rule that changes apply only to applications submitted after the effective date; avoid retroactive impacts on pending or completed certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must not construe 'other appropriate requirement of state law' so narrowly as to preclude non-discharge protective measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if 'other appropriate requirement of state law' is read to mean only EPA-approved CWA regulatory programs, states retain authority via section 301/303 to impose broader, non-discharge-based limits necessary to protect water quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule language and interpretive guidance must acknowledge and preserve states' independent authority to enforce section 303 standards and other state laws necessary to protect water quality under 401.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA must respect Supreme Court precedent and cannot displace unambiguous judicial interpretation without clear statutory ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: PUD No. 1 and S.D. Warren interpreted Section 401 and 'discharge' in ways that constrain agency reinterpretation. PUD No. 1 was effectively a Chevron step 1 decision; EPA has not shown ambiguity that would justify its proposed reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any proposed reinterpretation that conflicts with Supreme Court holdings requires careful justification and is likely unlawful if the Court's interpretation rested on the unambiguous statutory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must evaluate environmental consequences rather than dismissing impacts as speculative
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s analysis lacks evaluation of how the Proposed Rule would affect water quality across project types, and fails to show the proposed rule would be equally or more protective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule must include a reasoned, evidence-based assessment of environmental impacts, including concrete examples (mining, dams, pipeline spills) and quantified or qualitative harm where data exist.
